original_value: We focus on Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) for the task of semantic segmentation. Recently, adversarial alignment has been widely adopted to match the marginal distribution of feature representations across two domains globally. However, this strategy fails in adapting the representations of the tail classes or small objects for semantic segmentation since the alignment objective is dominated by head categories or large objects. In contrast to adversarial alignment, we propose to explicitly train a domain-invariant classifier by generating and defensing against pointwise feature space adversarial perturbations. Specifically, we firstly perturb the intermediate feature maps with several attack objectives (i.e., discriminator and classifier) on each individual position for both domains, and then the classifier is trained to be invariant to the perturbations. By perturbing each position individually, our model treats each location evenly regardless of the category or object size and thus circumvents the aforementioned issue. Moreover, the domain gap in feature space is reduced by extrapolating source and target perturbed features towards each other with attack on the domain discriminator. Our approach achieves the state-of-the-art performance on two challenging domain adaptation tasks for semantic segmentation: GTA5 → Cityscapes and SYNTHIA → Cityscapes.

result.paraphrase: We address unsupervised domain adaptation for semantic segmentation. Recent work has widely used adversarial alignment to globally match the marginal distributions of feature representations across two domains. Yet this approach is ineffective for adapting tail classes and small objects in semantic segmentation, because the alignment loss is dominated by head categories and large objects. Instead of adversarial alignment, we explicitly learn a domain-invariant classifier by generating pointwise adversarial perturbations in feature space and defending against them. Concretely, we first perturb intermediate feature maps at each individual position in both domains using multiple attack objectives, namely the discriminator and the classifier, and then train the classifier to be invariant to those perturbations. By attacking each position separately, our model weighs all locations equally regardless of category or object size, avoiding the issue above. In addition, we narrow the feature-space domain gap by pushing source and target perturbed features toward one another through attacks on the domain discriminator. Our method delivers state-of-the-art results on two challenging semantic segmentation domain adaptation benchmarks: GTA5 → Cityscapes and SYNTHIA → Cityscapes.
